summary: Analyzes security issues around DDP and RDMAP. It defines an architectural model for an RNIC, reviews attacks on its resources, and describes countermeasures. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RDMA lets a remote system access selected memory buffers directly, which can improve data transfer but exposes resources that need protection. RFC 5042 explains the main attacks and the safeguards an RNIC and its applications must provide.

subtitle: A security analysis of RDMA network resources, peer attacks and required countermeasures.

tldr.problem: Remote Direct Memory Access can let a peer place data directly in a host's memory. This creates risks to buffers, memory mappings and limited network-interface resources.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC models an RDMA-aware network interface, defines how streams and buffers may be shared, then analyzes attacks from the network, remote peers and local software. It gives required protections for the RNIC, resource manager and upper-layer protocol.
tldr.outcome: The RFC requires IPsec support as profiled by RFC 3723 and does not recommend TLS layered on DDP or RDMAP. Its metadata records an update by RFC 7146.

facts.label: Attack classes
facts.value: Spoofing, tampering, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege

today: RFC 5042 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007 and is updated by RFC 7146. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why RDMA Needs a Threat Model
sections.content:
Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) gives two endpoints more direct data-transfer options than ordinary stream or datagram communication. Direct Data Placement (DDP) and the Remote Direct Memory Access Protocol (RDMAP) can place received data into buffers chosen by the application. This flexibility creates security responsibilities for upper-layer protocols (ULPs) and RDMA-aware network interface controllers (RNICs).

The RFC groups threats into attacks requiring end-to-end security, attacks from remote peers and attacks from local peers. It considers spoofing, tampering, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. The aim is that implementations using the recommended protections should add no security weakness beyond the underlying transport and network protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: RDMA gives a peer controlled access to selected memory buffers. This RFC identifies how that access can be misused and which layers must prevent it.

sections.title: RNIC Components and Transfer Types
sections.content:
The model includes an RNIC Engine, a Privileged Resource Manager, and privileged and non-privileged ULPs. The Resource Manager allocates RNIC resources but does not send or receive data. A non-privileged ULP is untrusted; actions that could affect other ULPs must pass through a trusted intermediary.

DDP has two transfer forms. Untagged transfer places incoming data in the next buffer in a receive queue. Tagged transfer uses a Steering Tag (STag) to identify a destination buffer. The model also covers page translation tables, protection domains, completion queues, event queues and, for RDMAP, an RDMA Read Request Queue. A Protection Domain is local to the implementation and restricts which streams can use an STag.
sections.plainLanguage: The RNIC moves data, while a trusted resource manager controls access to memory mappings and other limited resources. A tagged transfer names its destination buffer with an STag.

sections.title: Trust, Sharing and Attacker Capabilities
sections.content:
The RFC treats local and remote peers as untrusted by default. Sharing resources across streams can save resources, but can also let one stream affect another. The term Partial Mutual Trust describes streams whose endpoints agree not to attack one another; a resource manager must not assume that trust without a mechanism that establishes it.

A connection must be established before DDP or RDMAP messages are transferred. An attacker outside the connection may need to guess transport parameters to send valid traffic. An attacker able to intercept and impersonate both endpoints has broader man-in-the-middle capabilities. For local software, non-privileged requests that affect other ULPs and requests for scarce resources must pass through the Privileged Resource Manager.
sections.plainLanguage: Sharing a buffer or queue is safe only when the streams that use it have the required trust relationship. The resource manager must verify permissions instead of assuming that applications trust one another.

sections.title: Network Attacks and End-to-End Protection
sections.content:
A network attacker may impersonate a peer, hijack a stream, alter buffer contents or read data in transit. The protections serve different purposes: confidentiality limits eavesdropping; per-packet authentication helps stop impersonation; integrity detects changes; and packet sequencing protects against replay.

The RFC requires RNIC implementations to follow the IPsec requirements in RFC 3723 Sections 2.3 and 5, including IPsec ESP mode. It does not recommend TLS on top of DDP or RDMAP: TLS can require TCP to collect out-of-order data before decryption, undermining flow-through transfer, and TLS above DDP/RDMAP does not protect their headers. Security must protect the connection end to end; an intermediate tunnel leaves the stream exposed between the endpoints and the tunnel device.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication, integrity, sequencing and confidentiality address different network attacks. The RFC requires the specified IPsec support and explains why TLS above DDP or RDMAP does not protect the protocol headers.

sections.title: Remote Peer Attacks on Buffers and Resources
sections.content:
A peer may try to use an STag on another stream, write outside a buffer, change a buffer after reporting completion, or read data that should not be exposed. The RNIC must enforce protection-domain and stream scope, check buffer bounds at byte granularity, and prevent further writes after an STag is revoked. ULPs should use hard-to-predict STags, revoke remote access before using received data, initialize buffers before granting read access, and grant only the needed access rights.

Different untrusted peers must not receive write access to the same buffer through different STags. Denial-of-service attacks can consume receive buffers, completion queues, read-request queues or other bounded RNIC resources. Scarce resources must be controlled by a Privileged Resource Manager. Shared queues need limits, appropriate sizing and mechanisms to detect unfair consumption; idle streams may be reclaimed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each remote buffer access needs a narrow range, the right permissions and a clear end point. The RNIC and resource manager must also stop one peer from consuming shared buffers or queues needed by others.

sections.title: Attacks from Local Peers and Server Rules
sections.content:
Local ULPs can also exhaust shared completion queues or RDMA Read Request Queues. An RNIC must not share a completion queue across ULPs that do not share Partial Mutual Trust. Interfaces that allocate read-request entries must be restricted to a trusted local peer, such as the Privileged Resource Manager, which should enforce fair use.

A non-privileged ULP must not directly map an STag to another ULP's memory. When non-privileged ULPs are supported, the resource manager must verify that the ULP may access a buffer before associating it with an STag. The normative client/server appendix further requires a server to revoke remote write access before acting on a peer-written buffer and to clear stale data before granting remote read access.
sections.plainLanguage: Software on the same host can attack shared queues and memory mappings. A trusted manager must check buffer ownership and prevent one application from taking another application's resources.

sections.title: Trust Models and Implementation Boundaries
sections.content:
The RFC describes five trust models based on whether local resources are shared, whether local ULPs trust one another, and whether they trust the remote peer. Models with no remote trust are typical for Internet communication; a model with shared resources and trust at both ends is intended for cooperating applications such as a cluster workload.

The document does not prescribe a particular RNIC implementation layout. Its resource and interface model is an abstraction, and its protections apply across implementations. The IANA section says that the document makes no IANA assignments.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementers choose a trust model that matches their applications and the resources they share. The detailed rules still apply even when a real RNIC organizes its components differently.

items.title: Data buffers
items.text: Memory exposed for local or remote transfer.

items.title: STags
items.text: Names used to authorize and locate tagged buffers.

items.title: Protection domains
items.text: Separate groups of resources and streams.

items.title: Completion queues
items.text: Hold notices that data operations completed.

items.title: Page translation tables
items.text: Map application buffer addresses for RNIC access.

items.title: Read request queue
items.text: Tracks RDMA Read requests before their responses finish.
